records.name: Huila
records.current_summary: Huila's file previously carried only methodology boilerplate about being assessed at the national position; stripped of that, the sourced reality is national: continuing killings of queer and trans people reported in an August 2025 investigation — in parts of the country, being queer means "to sign your own death sentence" — and a 2024 report of armed groups circulating "social cleansing" threats against trans women, with 41 trans women killed nationally in 2023 and more the following spring.  No Huila-specific statute, incident or protection mechanism appears in the audited sources. What a visitor can plan on is the national pattern of high lethality and near-total impunity; nothing on this record marks Huila as better or worse than that baseline.

sources.claim: CNN 'As Equals' investigation (6 Aug 2025), 'Viral video of her torture shocked Colombia. The killings didn't stop there': documents the continuing wave of killings of queer and trans people in Colombia after the Bello murder, and the framing that in parts of Colombia being queer means 'to sign your own death sentence'. National-context source; mostly a video/interactive feature with limited extractable body text.

The Guardian (30 Jul 2024) documented armed groups in Caquetá department running a 'social cleansing' campaign: flyers on the streets and via WhatsApp named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and a trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night; a second trans woman said a friend was killed. It reports eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and that discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. No Huila-specific finding appears; the national kill figures and the armed-group 'social-cleansing' pattern are the claims this record relies on.

The article records a Huila-specific outcome: in ruling T-268 of 2000 the Constitutional Court permitted a gay pride parade in Neiva, the department's capital, after the Mayor of Neiva had previously prevented it - establishing constitutional protection for public expression of sexual orientation in Huila. It also documents the national floor standing over the department: same-sex activity legal since 1981, orientation-based discrimination banned since 2011, same-sex marriage legal since April 2016, and legal gender change available since 1993 with birth-certificate markers F, M, NB and T. Nothing in the article marks Huila as diverging from that national framework.

records.name: Puno
records.current_summary: Puno has no regional statute or incident of its own in the audited record, and the decisive facts are national — which means they apply in Puno like anywhere in Peru. In February 2025, Congress's Women and Family Commission unanimously approved bills (6506 and 8457) barring trans people from using public restrooms corresponding to their gender identity, with narrow carve-outs for medical care, custody and accompanying minors or disabled persons; in April 2025 the plenary approved the fused measure, waiving a second vote. A national human-rights institute published a detailed critique calling the measure institutionalised discrimination.  For a trans visitor the mechanism is therefore legal, not customary: restroom access is the flashpoint the law itself creates — its trigger was a complaint about toilet signage at Lima's airport — with no local variation documented for Puno.

sources.claim: Infobae Perú (20 Feb 2025) reports the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion (dictamen) merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, barring trans people from public restrooms that do not correspond to their birth sex, with exceptions for custody, where medical attention is required, or accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities, plus a ban on 'ambiguous' bathroom signage; the trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint over the Jorge Chávez airport's gendered restroom labels. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho calls the measure discriminatory, warning that bathroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment (including ID checks), and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms. It contains no Puno-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding; for this record its value is the national ban on gender-matching restroom access that binds the region (committee stage, February 2025).

IDEHPUCP legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025) confirms that on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the congressional Plenary approved and exempted from second vote a bill whose article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', save for narrow listed exceptions, and argues this directly violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors say the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype implicitly presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors. It contains no Puno-specific finding; for this record its value is the human-rights institute's analysis of the national framework that governs the region.

records.name: Lambayeque
records.current_summary: No trans-specific regional law, ordinance or enforcement pattern is documented for Lambayeque; what binds a visitor here is the national framework. In February 2025 the congressional Women and Family Commission unanimously approved the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457, which bar trans people from public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex (narrow exceptions: custody, medical care, accompanying under-12s, the elderly or disabled) and prohibit ambiguous restroom signage; the plenary approved the fused text on 2 April 2025, waiving a second vote, and a university human-rights institute condemned Article 5.1 as legalized discrimination violating constitutional and inter-American equality guarantees.  Violence data is national only: the university TLGBI rights observatory recorded 54 LGBTI homicides and 170 rights-violation cases in 2020-2023 — over half of homicide victims trans women (30 of 54), 19 killings in 2023 alone — including a February 2023 case in which an extortion gang killed a trans sex worker in the capital. Enforcement would rest on individual staff checking IDs. The national machinery applies to Lambayeque in full.

sources.claim: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457 (sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante) that would prohibit any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions (custody, and cases where required, including accompanying minors, the elderly or people with disabilities), and would oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs; the article notes the text still needed plenary backing and reports the trigger as the July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho is quoted arguing the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender. This is the national framework this department is scored against; the article contains no Lambayeque-specific content.

IDEHPUCP legal analysis (15 April 2025, Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte): on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved and waived a second vote on the dictamen of the 'Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes', whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The institute reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination (Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights), resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, and recalls documented cases of trans people barred from public restrooms - including SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissing a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI - and the fact that gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive. This is the national framework this department is scored against; the article contains no Lambayeque-specific content.

Agencia Presentes (22 July 2024), drawing on the annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia: Peru recorded 54 assassinations of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in 2020-2023, the homicide victims being 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian; 19 killings occurred in 2023 alone (12 of them trans women), and killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides (13 of 19 in 2023). The piece recounts the February 2023 murder of trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano (31), kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots (Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot days earlier), with two killers arrested in March 2023, and notes the state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. This is the national violence baseline this department is scored against; the article contains no Lambayeque-specific content.
